newsitem.title: MAURITANIA: Opposition wins an assembly seat in Mauritania.
newsitem.headline: Opposition wins an assembly seat in Mauritania.

text.p: A new party championing the rights of Mauritania's blacks, ex-slaves and their descendants won a seat in the national assembly -- the first time the opposition has done so -- after a legislative election dominated by the ruling party.

Final results, released by the interior ministry on Saturday, also showed women entering the Moslem West African nation's 79-seat assembly for the first time -- with a winner from each of the two rounds.

Former gendarme Kebe Abdoulaye, from Mauritania's black community, will represent the year-old Action for Change party and the capital Nouakchott's Sebha district in the new assembly, the second since Mauritania's 1991 democratic transition.
The ruling Democratic and Social Republican Party, which won a crushing first round majority amid cries of fraud, mopped up many of the remaining seats in the Friday runoffs to boost its tally to 71.
Independents, mostly ruling party supporters passed over for the party ticket, won six seats, and a small party supporting President Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya won one.
One of the two women, Lalla Zeina Mint Sbaghou, is a member of the ruling party and but also a Harratin, or descendent of the slaves once held by the dominant light-skinned Moors.
The other, Malado Coulibaly, is an independent who defeated the head of the ruling party caucus in the outgoing assembly.
The October 11 first round was the first truly multi-party legislative election in the former French colony straddling Arab and black Africa,
The opposition boycotted the first such election in 1992, alleging widespread fraud after Taya, who seized power in a bloodless 1984 coup, won a six-year term.
Action for Change was the only opposition party represented in Friday's second round.

Veteran opposition stalwart Ahmed Ould Daddah, who alleged massive fraud in the first round, pulled his Union of Democratic Forces-New Era party out of the runoffs, passing up the chance of winning two seats in Nouakchott. The ruling party won both.

Action for Change, formed just over a year ago and led by former slave Messoud Ould Boulkheir, had the backing of Ould Daddah's party and the moderate Union for Democracy and Progress. Witnesses described turnout in the capital as low.
Mauritania, a sparsely populated nation of 2.2 million people, stands at the Atlantic fringe of the Sahara Desert.
Moors of Arab stock and blacks each make up a third of the population and Harratin the remainder. Mauritania formally banned slavery in 1980.
International observers spoke of "imperfections" in the first round, in which the opposition had been hoping to make its mark ahead of a presidential election due by January 1998.

Rivalry between Moors and black Mauritanians spilled over into tension with neighbouring Senegal and bloodshed in 1989. Migrant Moors and Harratins were killed in race riots in Senegal and there were reprisal killings in Mauritania.
The rise of Action for Change has put the racial divide, which has plagued Mauritania since independence in 1960, firmly back on the agenda.
Politicians say that for the first time Harratin, who historically consider themselves part of the Arab community with the Moors, have made common cause with blacks from the south.
